• Heart rate: 60–100 bpm
• Rhythm: regular, sinoatrial origin (sinus rhythm)
• Cardiac axis: −30° to +90°
• P waves present; each P wave followed by a QRS complex
• PR interval: 120–200 ms (3–5 small squares)
• QRS: <0.12 s, normal morphology and chest-lead progression
• ST segment flat/isoelectric
• T waves usually upright; inversion in V1 and in III is a normal variant

• Heart rate: >100 bpm (typically 100–180 bpm)
• Rhythm: regular, sinoatrial origin
• P waves visible before each QRS (may overlap preceding T wave at high rates)
• PR interval normal or mildly shortened
• QRS: normal morphology (<0.12 s)
• Common causes: exercise, fever, anxiety, hypovolaemia, hyperthyroidism

• Heart rate: <60 bpm
• Rhythm: regular, sinoatrial origin
• P waves present; each P wave followed by a QRS complex
• All intervals within normal limits
• Often physiological (trained athletes, sleep, high vagal tone)
• Treat if symptomatic: syncope, hypotension, or effort intolerance
Irregular rhythm, absent P waves · ~88 bpm

• Heart rate: variable, 60–180 bpm (untreated)
• Rhythm: irregularly irregular
• No identifiable P waves; fibrillatory baseline (f waves, best seen in V1)
• Variable RR intervals
• QRS usually narrow (<0.12 s)
• Most common sustained arrhythmia; significant thromboembolic risk

• No recognisable PQRST complexes
• Chaotic high-frequency oscillations with variable amplitude
• Life-threatening emergency — cardiac output ceases immediately
• No effective pulse is generated
• Immediate treatment: electrical defibrillation + CPR
• Precipitated by acute MI, hypoxia, or severe electrolyte disturbances
The electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart\'s electrical activity. Each cardiac cycle produces a characteristic pattern of five waves: P, Q, R, S, and T. Tap each section to learn more.

The P wave represents electrical activation of the atria, initiated by the sinoatrial (SA) node and spreading through both atria to trigger their contraction.

• Normal duration: 80–120 ms
• Amplitude: < 2.5 mm
• Positive in leads I, II, and aVF
• Inversion in aVR is normal

The QRS complex represents ventricular depolarisation via the His-Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium.

• Q wave: septal depolarisation (small, negative)
• R wave: free ventricular wall (large, positive)
• S wave: basal regions (negative)
• Normal duration: < 120 ms
• QRS ≥ 120 ms suggests bundle branch block

The T wave represents electrical recovery (repolarisation) of the ventricles.

• Asymmetric shape: slow rise, rapid descent
• Polarity concordant with QRS
• Inversion in V1 and lead III may be normal
• Inversion in V2–V6 suggests ischaemia or hypertrophy

Time from onset of atrial depolarisation to onset of ventricular depolarisation. Reflects the physiological delay in the AV node.

• Normal: 120–200 ms
• Short PR: pre-excitation (WPW) or junctional rhythm
• Long PR (> 200 ms): first-degree AV block
• Variable PR: second or third-degree AV block

From the end of the QRS (J-point) to the start of the T wave. Normally isoelectric (flat at baseline).

• ST elevation (> 1 mm): acute MI, pericarditis
• ST depression (> 0.5 mm): subendocardial ischaemia, digoxin effect

⚠ Educational only — does not replace clinical diagnosis

Total duration of ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation. Rate-dependent — corrected with Bazett's formula.

• QTc = QT / √RR
• Normal QTc: < 440 ms (♂) / < 460 ms (♀)
• QTc > 500 ms: increased risk of torsade de pointes
• Causes: drugs, hypokalaemia, hypocalcaemia
The heart has four chambers and a specialised electrical system that coordinates its contraction. Understanding this system helps interpret the ECG.
RA: Right Atrium · LA: Left Atrium · RV: Right Ventricle · LV: Left Ventricle
The natural pacemaker of the heart

Located in the upper wall of the right atrium (RA), the SA node generates spontaneous electrical impulses that initiate each heartbeat.

• Intrinsic rate: 60–100 bpm at rest
• Regulated by the autonomic nervous system
• Produces the P wave on the ECG
• Dysfunction: sick sinus syndrome (sinus bradycardia, sinus arrest)

Located in the interatrial septum, the AV node is the only normal electrical bridge between the atria and ventricles. It introduces a 120–200 ms delay.

• Escape rate: 40–60 bpm
• The delay allows the atria to empty before ventricular systole
• Reflects the PR interval on the ECG
• AV block: 1st degree (long PR), 2nd degree (dropped beats), 3rd degree (AV dissociation)

The bundle of His descends through the interventricular septum and splits into a right bundle branch (to RV) and left bundle branch (to LV, with anterior and posterior fascicles).

• Escape rate: 20–40 bpm
• Conduction velocity: ~2 m/s
• RBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rSR' in V1
• LBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, characteristic morphology in V5–V6

A dense network of highly specialised fibres that distribute the impulse almost simultaneously across the ventricular subendocardium, ensuring efficient contraction.

• Fastest conduction in the heart: ~4 m/s
• Synchronised activation of ventricular myocardium
• Escape rate: 20–40 bpm
• Produces the QRS complex on the ECG

The impulse from the SA node spreads through the atria via preferential pathways (Bachmann's bundle, anterior, middle, and posterior tracts) to the AV node.

• Velocity: ~1 m/s in atrial myocardium
• Bachmann's bundle conducts the impulse to the left atrium
• Atrial propagation generates the P wave
• Normal duration: 80–120 ms
